claim: Epithelial cells possess intrinsic mechanisms to maintain an appropriate cell density for normal tissue morphogenesis and homeostasis.
source: Epithelial cells possess intrinsic mechanisms to maintain an appropriate cell density for normal tissue morphogenesis and homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about epithelial cell biology that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Defects in density-dependent proliferation mechanisms likely contribute to hyperplasia and cancer initiation.
source: Defects in such mechanisms likely contribute to hyperplasia and cancer initiation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the consequences of defects in density-dependent proliferation mechanisms.

claim: A genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen was performed to identify genes that regulate density-dependent proliferation of murine mammary epithelial cells.
source: To identify genes that regulate the density-dependent proliferation of murine mammary epithelial cells, we developed a fluorescence-activated cell sorting assay based on fluorescence ubiquitination cell cycle indicator, which marks different stages of the cell cycle with distinct fluorophores. Using this powerful assay, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen, selecting for cells that proliferate normally at low density but continue to divide at high density.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Traf3 was identified as a top hit in the CRISPR screen.
source: Unexpectedly, one top hit was Traf3, a negative regulator of NF-κB signaling that has never previously been linked to density-dependent proliferation.
evidence: This is a direct result from the CRISPR screen data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRAF3 is a negative regulator of NF-κB signaling.
source: Unexpectedly, one top hit was Traf3, a negative regulator of NF-κB signaling that has never previously been linked to density-dependent proliferation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRAF3 function.

claim: TRAF3 has never previously been linked to density-dependent proliferation.
source: Unexpectedly, one top hit was Traf3, a negative regulator of NF-κB signaling that has never previously been linked to density-dependent proliferation.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on existing literature.

claim: Loss of Traf3 specifically activates noncanonical NF-κB signaling.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Traf3 specifically activates noncanonical NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated through multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of noncanonical NF-κB signaling triggers an innate immune response.
source: This in turn triggers an innate immune response and drives cell division independently of known density-dependent proliferation mechanisms, including YAP/TAZ signaling and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, by blocking entry into quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data showing upregulation of immune response genes.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 drives cell division independently of YAP/TAZ signaling.
source: This in turn triggers an innate immune response and drives cell division independently of known density-dependent proliferation mechanisms, including YAP/TAZ signaling and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, by blocking entry into quiescence.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing YAP localization and target gene expression are not affected by TRAF3 loss.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 drives cell division independently of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors.
source: This in turn triggers an innate immune response and drives cell division independently of known density-dependent proliferation mechanisms, including YAP/TAZ signaling and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, by blocking entry into quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing no changes in CKI levels.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 blocks entry into quiescence.
source: This in turn triggers an innate immune response and drives cell division independently of known density-dependent proliferation mechanisms, including YAP/TAZ signaling and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, by blocking entry into quiescence.
evidence: This is demonstrated through DHB-mVenus localization and phospho-RB staining experiments.

claim: Epithelial cells do not undergo contact inhibition but continue to proliferate at confluence.
source: An important characteristic of epithelial cells is that, unlike fibroblasts, they do not undergo contact inhibition but continue to proliferate at confluence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epithelial cell behavior.

claim: Epithelial cell proliferation terminates at a preset cell density.
source: Importantly, however, proliferation is not indefinite but terminates at a preset cell density (Fomicheva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Stretching or wounding an epithelial sheet can reinitiate cell division.
source: Stretching or wounding an epithelial sheet, which reduces the cell density, can reinitiate cell division (Aragona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Compression of epithelial cells can result in extrusion and apoptosis to maintain homeostatic state.
source: Conversely, compression, which increases density, can result in extrusion and apoptosis of cells so as to bring the epithelial layer back to its homeostatic state (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The control mechanism that prevents tissue overgrowth is essential for normal development and is lost in hyperplasia and cancer.
source: This control mechanism that prevents tissue overgrowth is essential for normal development, and it is lost in hyperplasia and in cancer.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: The mechanisms that underlie homeostatic cell density maintenance remain incompletely understood.
source: However, the mechanisms that underlie homeostatic cell density maintenance remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: YAP and TAZ are transcriptional co-activators that are nuclear at low cell density or under conditions of high mechanical strain.
source: These transcriptional co-activators are nuclear at low cell density or under conditions of high mechanical strain, but become phosphorylated and are cytoplasmic (or junction-associated) and nonfunctional at high density and/or low strain (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: YAP and TAZ become phosphorylated and are cytoplasmic and nonfunctional at high density and/or low strain.
source: These transcriptional co-activators are nuclear at low cell density or under conditions of high mechanical strain, but become phosphorylated and are cytoplasmic (or junction-associated) and nonfunctional at high density and/or low strain (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: LGL1/2 can control density-dependent proliferation by inhibiting proteasomal degradation of p27.
source: Independently of YAP/TAZ, however, the polarity proteins LGL1/2 can also control density-dependent proliferation by inhibiting proteasomal degradation of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor (CKI) CDKN1B (p27).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Loss of LGL1/2 reduces the expression of p27.
source: Loss of LGL1/2 reduces the expression of p27, which is often upregulated at high cell density to arrest proliferation (Yamashita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: p27 is often upregulated at high cell density to arrest proliferation.
source: Loss of LGL1/2 reduces the expression of p27, which is often upregulated at high cell density to arrest proliferation (Yamashita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Other Hippo pathway components and/or currently unknown Hippo-independent signaling mechanisms likely exist.
source: It is, therefore, likely that other Hippo pathway components and/or currently unknown Hippo-independent signaling mechanisms exist; however, no strategy has been designed to identify such mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the complexity of the pathway and recent findings.

claim: The FUCCI system marks proliferating cells in S/G2/M phases with green fluorescent protein and cells in G1/G0 with red fluorescent protein.
source: The screen employs a fluorescence ubiquitination cell cycle indicator (FUCCI) system to mark proliferating cells in S/G2/M phases of cell cycle with a green fluorescent protein, and cells in G1/G0 with a red fluorescent protein (Sladitschek and Neveu, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the FUCCI system supported by a citation.

claim: Mammary EpH4 epithelial cells robustly arrest in G1 or G0 by 4 days post-confluency.
source: We found that mammary EpH4 epithelial cells robustly arrest in G1 or G0 by 4 days post-confluency.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Nf2 (Merlin) was the top hit from the CRISPR screen.
source: The top hit was Nf2 (also called Merlin), a known tumor suppressor that negatively regulates YAP/TAZ, which validated our approach (Petrilli and Fernández-Valle, 2016).
evidence: This is a direct result from the screen data.

claim: NF2 is a known tumor suppressor that negatively regulates YAP/TAZ.
source: The top hit was Nf2 (also called Merlin), a known tumor suppressor that negatively regulates YAP/TAZ, which validated our approach (Petrilli and Fernández-Valle, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TRAF3 is critical for lymphocyte proliferation control and immune responses.
source: TRAF3 (TNF receptor associated factor 3) is critical for lymphocyte proliferation control and immune responses (Zapata et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TRAF3 negatively regulates signaling through multiple pathways, including the canonical and noncanonical NF-κB pathways.
source: It negatively regulates signaling through multiple pathways, including the canonical and noncanonical NF-κB pathways (He et al., 2006; Ramakrishnan et al., 2004; Zarnegar et al., 2008; Sun, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deletions and mutations of TRAF3 are among the most common genetic alterations in human B cell malignancies.
source: Deletions and mutations of TRAF3 are among the most common genetic alterations in human B cell malignancies (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: B cell-specific KO of the Traf3 gene in mice leads to increased B cell numbers and spontaneous lymphomas.
source: B cell-specific KO of the Traf3 gene in mice leads to increased B cell numbers and spontaneous lymphomas (Moore et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Myeloid-specific Traf3 KO causes histiocytic sarcomas of macrophage origin.
source: Myeloid-specific Traf3 KO causes histiocytic sarcomas of macrophage origin (Lalani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TRAF3 is critical for the prevention of malignant growth in blood cells.
source: Therefore, TRAF3 is critical for the prevention of malignant growth in blood cells; however, TRAF3 roles in epithelia have not yet been widely investigated, despite its ubiquitous expression in mouse and human tissues (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies and supported by a citation about expression.

claim: TRAF3 roles in epithelia have not yet been widely investigated.
source: Therefore, TRAF3 is critical for the prevention of malignant growth in blood cells; however, TRAF3 roles in epithelia have not yet been widely investigated, despite its ubiquitous expression in mouse and human tissues (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: TRAF3 is ubiquitously expressed in mouse and human tissues.
source: Therefore, TRAF3 is critical for the prevention of malignant growth in blood cells; however, TRAF3 roles in epithelia have not yet been widely investigated, despite its ubiquitous expression in mouse and human tissues (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: UBE2M is a NEDD8 conjugation E2 enzyme that neddylates CULLIN-RING ligases to stimulate their activity.
source: UBE2M is a NEDD8 conjugation E2 enzyme, which neddylates CULLIN-RING ligases to stimulate their activity (Lydeard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Stress induces UBE2M expression and promotes its ubiquitylation of UBE2F, the degradation of which can suppress cell proliferation.
source: Interestingly, stress induces UBE2M expression and promotes its ubiquitylation of UBE2F, the degradation of which can suppress cell proliferation (Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of NF2, TRAF3, or UBE2M results in increased cell proliferation at high density.
source: Loss of any of these genes results in increased cell proliferation at high density and multilayering of cells; however, proliferation at low cell density remains unaltered.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays and imaging.

claim: Loss of NF2, TRAF3, or UBE2M causes multilayering of cells at high density.
source: Loss of any of these genes results in increased cell proliferation at high density and multilayering of cells; however, proliferation at low cell density remains unaltered.
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal imaging.

claim: Proliferation at low cell density remains unaltered in NF2, TRAF3, or UBE2M knockout cells.
source: Loss of any of these genes results in increased cell proliferation at high density and multilayering of cells; however, proliferation at low cell density remains unaltered.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays.

claim: Only about 1% of EpH4-FUCCI cells express mCitrine at 4 days post-confluency.
source: As expected, the EpH4-FUCCI cells remain proliferative at 1 day post-confluency but very few cells cycle at high density, with only about 1% of cells expressing mCitrine at 4 days post-confluency (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Depletion of p27 increases cell proliferation after 4 days post-confluency in EpH4-FUCCI cells.
source: The p27-depleted cells display increased cell proliferation after 4 days post-confluency in contrast to cells expressing scrambled shRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through FACS analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The GeCKO CRISPR v2 KO library contains six sgRNAs against each of 20,611 genes, plus 1000 non-targeting controls, for a total of 130,209 sgRNAs.
source: The library contains six sgRNAs against each of 20,611 genes, plus 1000 non-targeting controls, for a total of 130,209 sgRNAs.
evidence: This is a description of the library used in the screen.

claim: EpH4-FUCCI cells were transduced with viruses at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.3 to ensure cells would receive only one sgRNA on average.
source: To ensure that our EpH4-FUCCI cells would receive only one sgRNA on average, we transduced cells with viruses at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The screen was designed to maintain 150-300 cells per sgRNA in each step.
source: Therefore, we aimed to have 150–300 cells per sgRNA in each step of the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Three rounds of FACS sorting were performed in the screen.
source: In total, we performed three FAC sorts.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: There was a steady increase in the number of mCitrine+ cells after each round of FACS.
source: We observed a steady increase in the number of mCitrine+ cells after each round of FACS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen data shown in the figures.

claim: Nf2/Merlin was the top enriched target in the screen.
source: Interestingly, the top enriched target was Nf2/Merlin, which is a known tumor suppressor gene and a regulator of Hippo signaling necessary for cell density control (Petrilli and Fernández-Valle, 2016).
evidence: This is a direct result from the screen analysis.

claim: sgRNAs for Nf2 were enriched by >1000× above the control abundance.
source: This hit, the sgRNAs for which were enriched by >1000× above the control abundance, strongly validated our screening strategy.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the screen data.

claim: Traf3 and Ube2m have not previously been implicated in density-dependent cell cycle arrest.
source: Two unexpected hits were for the Traf3 and Ube2m (Ubс12) genes (Figure 1G), which have not previously been implicated in density-dependent cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings based on existing literature.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 results in cell overgrowth in both mouse and human mammary gland cell lines.
source: We discovered that loss of TRAF3 results in cell overgrowth in both mouse and human mammary gland cell lines, and mesenchymal cells (NIH 3T3 fibroblasts) as well as in primary mouse mammary gland organoids.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple experiments in different cell types.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 results in cell overgrowth in mesenchymal cells (NIH 3T3 fibroblasts).
source: We discovered that loss of TRAF3 results in cell overgrowth in both mouse and human mammary gland cell lines, and mesenchymal cells (NIH 3T3 fibroblasts) as well as in primary mouse mammary gland organoids.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays in NIH 3T3 cells.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 results in cell overgrowth in primary mouse mammary gland organoids.
source: We discovered that loss of TRAF3 results in cell overgrowth in both mouse and human mammary gland cell lines, and mesenchymal cells (NIH 3T3 fibroblasts) as well as in primary mouse mammary gland organoids.
evidence: This is demonstrated through organoid experiments showing increased mitotic index.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 specifically activates the noncanonical branch of NF-κB signaling.
source: We interrogated the mechanism of TRAF3-dependent proliferation control in mammary gland epithelial cells (Figure 9) and found that loss of TRAF3 specifically activates the noncanonical branch of NF-κB signaling, while having no effect on canonical NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RELB localization, p100/p52 processing, and p65 localization experiments.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 has no effect on canonical NF-κB signaling.
source: We interrogated the mechanism of TRAF3-dependent proliferation control in mammary gland epithelial cells (Figure 9) and found that loss of TRAF3 specifically activates the noncanonical branch of NF-κB signaling, while having no effect on canonical NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through p65 localization and IκB degradation experiments.

claim: The noncanonical NF-κB pathway is necessary for over-proliferation at high density in cells lacking TRAF3.
source: We further discovered that the noncanonical pathway is necessary for over-proliferation at high density in cells lacking TRAF3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through p100 and NIK knockout experiments in TRAF3 KO cells.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 does not induce the transcription of classical proliferation pathway components, including YAP/TAZ, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, TGF-β, and WNT signaling.
source: Our RNAseq data revealed that loss of TRAF3 does not induce the transcription of classical proliferation pathway components, including YAP/TAZ, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, TGF-β, and WNT signaling.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq and IPA analysis.

claim: Over-proliferation caused by loss of TRAF3 is cell autonomous.
source: We also demonstrated that over-proliferation caused by loss of TRAF3 is cell autonomous, as control cells did not over-proliferate when co-cultured with TRAF3 KO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-culture experiments with labeled cells.

claim: No differences in levels of p27 or other CKIs (p21, p19, and p18) were found in cells lacking TRAF3 versus control EpH4 cells.
source: However, we found no differences in levels of p27 or other CKIs (p21, p19, and p18) in cells lacking TRAF3 versus control EpH4 cells, although p21 levels do increase with increased cell density.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: p21 levels increase with increased cell density.
source: However, we found no differences in levels of p27 or other CKIs (p21, p19, and p18) in cells lacking TRAF3 versus control EpH4 cells, although p21 levels do increase with increased cell density.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 prevents cells from entering quiescent state G0.
source: Nonetheless, our data demonstrate that loss of TRAF3 prevents cells from entering quiescent state G0 as shown by increased CDK2 activity and RB phosphorylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through DHB-mVenus localization and phospho-RB staining experiments.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 leads to the activation of immune response pathways, at least in part through noncanonical NF-κB signaling.
source: RNAseq analysis revealed that loss of TRAF3 leads to the activation of immune response pathways, at least in part through noncanonical NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data comparing TRAF3 KO and TRAF3/p100 double KO cells.

claim: Activated genes in TRAF3 KO cells include antigen presentation, interferon response pathways, and genes responsible for foreign DNA and RNA recognition.
source: Activated genes include antigen presentation, interferon response pathways, and genes responsible for foreign DNA and RNA recognition.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq and IPA analysis.

claim: Expression of antigen presentation, interferon response, and foreign DNA/RNA recognition genes was reduced when p100 was deleted in TRAF3 KO cells.
source: Expression of these genes was reduced when p100 was deleted in theTRAF3 KO cells.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data comparing TRAF3 KO and TRAF3/p100 double KO cells.

claim: Certain genes induced in the TRAF3 KO cells, including adhesion molecules, superoxide-producing enzymes, and chemokines, were not reduced by deletion of p100.
source: However, certain genes induced in the TRAF3 KO cells, including adhesion molecules, superoxide-producing enzymes, and chemokines, were not reduced by deletion of p100.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data comparing TRAF3 KO and TRAF3/p100 double KO cells.

claim: A mechanism independent of noncanonical NF-κB signaling can drive gene expression responses activated by loss of TRAF3.
source: These data reveal that a mechanism independent of noncanonical NF-κB signaling can drive gene expression responses activated by loss of TRAF3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAseq data showing some genes are not affected by p100 deletion.

claim: Helicobacter pylori activates noncanonical NF-κB signaling in a stomach epithelial cell line and in H. pylori-associated gastritis.
source: Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium associated with the development of gastritis and gastric cancer, activates noncanonical NF-κB signaling in a stomach epithelial cell line and in H. pylori-associated gastritis (Feige et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Activation of the noncanonical NF-κB pathway in response to infection correlates with hyperplasia of the ear mucosa following otitis infection.
source: Moreover, activation of the noncanonical NF-κB pathway in response to infection correlates with hyperplasia of the ear mucosa following otitis infection, although the mechanism was not investigated (Cho et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Traf3 is mutated, though at low frequency, in different cancers of epithelial origin.
source: As discussed above, Traf3 is mutated, though at low frequency, in different cancers of epithelial origin (Zhu et al., 2018), and low expression is associated with worse outcomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Low Traf3 expression is associated with worse outcomes in cancer patients.
source: As discussed above, Traf3 is mutated, though at low frequency, in different cancers of epithelial origin (Zhu et al., 2018), and low expression is associated with worse outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Noncanonical NF-κB signaling is associated with different epithelial cancers, including breast cancer and lung cancer.
source: Noncanonical NF-κB signaling is also associated with different epithelial cancers, including breast cancer (Sovak et al., 1997; Rojo et al., 2016) and lung cancer (Dimitrakopoulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TRAF3 KO organoids formed multilayered buds with small or no detectable lumens.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, WT organoids form buds with hollow lumens, but organoids lacking TRAF3 formed multilayered buds with small or no detectable lumens.
evidence: This is an observation from organoid experiments shown in the figure.

claim: TRAF3 KO organoids had a substantially higher mitotic index compared to control organoids.
source: Additionally, staining for phospho-HISTONE H3 revealed a substantially higher mitotic index in organoids deleted for Traf3, compared to organoids transduced with a control sgRNA (Figure 3B and C), demonstrating that TRAF3 normally suppresses WT tissue overgrowth.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of pH3-positive cells in organoids.

claim: TRAF3 normally suppresses wild-type tissue overgrowth.
source: Additionally, staining for phospho-HISTONE H3 revealed a substantially higher mitotic index in organoids deleted for Traf3, compared to organoids transduced with a control sgRNA (Figure 3B and C), demonstrating that TRAF3 normally suppresses WT tissue overgrowth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the organoid data showing increased proliferation when TRAF3 is deleted.

claim: MCF10a TRAF3 KO cells over-proliferate at high density.
source: We assessed cell proliferation by immunofluorescence and cytometric analysis of BrdU incorporation as described above, and found that, similar to EpH4 cells, MCF10a TRAF3 KO cells, but not WT MCF10a cells, over-proliferate at high density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and B′).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays in MCF10a cells.

claim: CRISPR KO of Traf3 in NIH 3T3 fibroblasts promoted cell proliferation at high density.
source: CRISPR KO of Traf3 (confirmed by western blotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and D')) promoted cell proliferation at high density as measured by cytometric analysis of BrdU staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and D').
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays in NIH 3T3 cells.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 broadly interferes with cell cycle arrest including cells of epithelial and mesenchymal lineages.
source: These data suggest that loss of TRAF3 broadly interferes with cell cycle arrest including cells of epithelial and mesenchymal lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from multiple cell types.

claim: In the noncanonical NF-κB pathway, TRAF3 constitutively promotes proteasomal degradation of MAP3K14 (NIK).
source: In the noncanonical pathway, TRAF3 constitutively promotes proteasomal degradation of MAP3K14 (NIK), a kinase that is essential for activation of the downstream signaling cascade.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the noncanonical NF-κB pathway.

claim: Ligand recruitment to an upstream receptor triggers TRAF3 poly-ubiquitinylation and degradation.
source: Ligand recruitment to an upstream receptor triggers TRAF3 poly-ubiquitinylation and degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the noncanonical NF-κB pathway.

claim: When TRAF3 is degraded, NIK levels increase and it phosphorylates its downstream target IKKα.
source: As a result, NIK levels increase, and it phosphorylates its downstream target IKKα, which in turn phosphorylates NFKB2 (p100).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the noncanonical NF-κB pathway.

claim: Phosphorylated p100 is partially degraded to p52, which enters the nucleus in association with RELB.
source: Phosphorylated p100 is partially degraded to p52, which enters the nucleus in association with RELB and regulates the transcription of target genes (Sun, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the noncanonical NF-κB pathway supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 caused a substantial nuclear accumulation of RELB in EpH4 cells.
source: As expected, RELB was predominantly cytoplasmic in control cells and organoids. However, loss of TRAF3 caused a substantial nuclear accumulation, indicative of noncanonical NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence staining of RELB.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 caused a substantial nuclear accumulation of RELB in primary mammary gland organoids.
source: As expected, RELB was predominantly cytoplasmic in control cells and organoids. However, loss of TRAF3 caused a substantial nuclear accumulation, indicative of noncanonical NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence staining of RELB in organoids.

claim: TRAF3 KO cells at both 1 and 4 days post-confluency had substantially increased NIK levels compared to NT control cells.
source: TRAF3 KO cells at both 1 and 4 days post-confluency had substantially increased NIK levels and enhanced processing of p100 to p52 compared to NT control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: TRAF3 KO cells at both 1 and 4 days post-confluency had enhanced processing of p100 to p52 compared to NT control cells.
source: TRAF3 KO cells at both 1 and 4 days post-confluency had substantially increased NIK levels and enhanced processing of p100 to p52 compared to NT control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: Cell density differences had no impact on NIK, RELB, TRAF3, and p100/p52 protein levels.
source: However, cell density differences had no impact on NIK, RELB, TRAF3, and p100/p52 protein levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments comparing low and high density.

claim: TRAF3 KO leads to activation of noncanonical NF-κB signaling, but regulation of these pathway components is independent of cell density.
source: Therefore, TRAF3 KO leads to activation of noncanonical NF-κB signaling, but regulation of these pathway components is independent of cell density.
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blotting data showing no density-dependent changes.

claim: RELA/p65 did not accumulate in the nuclei of TRAF3 KO cells.
source: Surprisingly, however, RELA/p65 did not accumulate in the nuclei of TRAF3 KO cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence staining of p65.

claim: No IκB degradation was observed in control and TRAF3 KO cells either at low or at high density.
source: Immunoblotting for the canonical NF-κB pathway components showed activation of IKKα/β phosphorylation at high density in both control and TRAF3 KO cells, but no IκB degradation was observed in control and TRAF3 KO cells either at low or at high density (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: In mammary epithelial cells, the loss of TRAF3 specifically activates noncanonical but not canonical NF-κB signaling.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that in mammary epithelial cells, the loss of TRAF3 specifically activates noncanonical but not canonical NF-κB signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RELB, p100/p52, and p65 localization and western blotting data.

claim: Deletion of p100 in TRAF3 KO cells substantially reduced proliferation compared to TRAF3 KO cells.
source: The proliferation of TRAF3/p100 double KO cells was, however, substantially reduced compared to TRAF3 KO cells (Figure 5C and D) demonstrating that noncanonical NF-κB signaling is required for the phenotype induced by loss of TRAF3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays.

claim: Noncanonical NF-κB signaling is required for the phenotype induced by loss of TRAF3.
source: The proliferation of TRAF3/p100 double KO cells was, however, substantially reduced compared to TRAF3 KO cells (Figure 5C and D) demonstrating that noncanonical NF-κB signaling is required for the phenotype induced by loss of TRAF3.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the p100 knockout rescue experiment.

claim: Deletion of NIK caused reduced proliferation in TRAF3 KO cells.
source: Similar to p100 KO, deletion of NIK caused reduced proliferation in TRAF3 KO cells (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays in TRAF3/NIK double KO cells.

claim: Treatment with BV6 induces over-proliferation of NT cells at high density but not at low density.
source: We treated cells with BV6 at low and high density (Figure 5H and I, respectively) and observed that BV6 treatment induces over-proliferation of NT cells at high density but not at low density, as shown by cytometric analysis of BrdU staining (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays with BV6 treatment.

claim: Overexpression of NIK-ΔT3 causes strong over-proliferation of NT cells at 4 days post-confluency compared to NT control cells.
source: Flow cytometry and immunofluorescent staining showed strong over-proliferation of NT NIK-ΔT3 cells at 4 days post-confluency compared to NT control cells (Figure 5K and L) demonstrating that activation of noncanonical NF-κB pathway is sufficient for increased proliferation at high density.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays in cells overexpressing NIK-ΔT3.

claim: Activation of noncanonical NF-κB pathway is sufficient for increased proliferation at high density.
source: Flow cytometry and immunofluorescent staining showed strong over-proliferation of NT NIK-ΔT3 cells at 4 days post-confluency compared to NT control cells (Figure 5K and L) demonstrating that activation of noncanonical NF-κB pathway is sufficient for increased proliferation at high density.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NIK-ΔT3 overexpression experiment.

claim: TRAF3 normally suppresses proliferation at high cell density via inhibition of the noncanonical NF-κB pathway but does not impact proliferation at lower cell density.
source: We conclude that TRAF3 normally suppresses proliferation at high cell density via inhibition of the noncanonical NF-κB pathway but does not impact proliferation at lower cell density.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The noncanonical NF-κB pathway does not contribute to proliferation in WT EpH4 cells but is constitutively activated by loss of TRAF3.
source: This pathway does not contribute to proliferation in WT EpH4 cells but is constitutively activated by loss of TRAF3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no density-dependent changes in pathway components in WT cells.

claim: Activation of noncanonical NF-κB pathway downstream of TRAF3 is both necessary and sufficient for over-proliferation phenotype at high density.
source: Activation of noncanonical NF-κB pathway downstream of TRAF3 is both necessary and sufficient for over-proliferation phenotype at high density.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the p100/NIK knockout and NIK-ΔT3 overexpression experiments.

claim: Gene expression changes downstream of noncanonical NF-κB signaling have not been investigated in epithelia.
source: However, gene expression changes downstream of noncanonical NF-κB signaling have not been investigated in epithelia, nor is it known which genes are targets of p52 in epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It is not known which genes are targets of p52 in epithelial cells.
source: However, gene expression changes downstream of noncanonical NF-κB signaling have not been investigated in epithelia, nor is it known which genes are targets of p52 in epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: IPA did not detect any stimulation by TRAF3 KO of those signaling pathways classically involved in proliferation, including PI3K/AKT, JNK, TGF-β, WNT, and Hippo.
source: Surprisingly, IPA did not detect any stimulation by TRAF3 KO of those signaling pathways classically involved in proliferation, including PI3K/AKT, JNK, TGF-β, WNT, and Hippo (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on IPA analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: There was a dramatic induction of innate immune response genes by deletion of TRAF3.
source: There was, however, a dramatic induction of innate immune response genes.
evidence: This is based on IPA analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: Antigen presentation, interferon response genes, and genes responsible for foreign DNA and RNA recognition were strongly upregulated by deletion of TRAF3.
source: Antigen presentation, interferon response genes, and genes responsible for foreign DNA and RNA recognition were strongly upregulated by deletion of TRAF3 (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data and shown in heatmaps.

claim: TRAF3 KO cells overexpress adhesion molecules Icam1 and Vcam1.
source: Additionally, TRAF3 KO cells overexpress adhesion molecules Icam1 and Vcam1 that facilitate adhesion of recruited leukocytes (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data shown in heatmaps.

claim: Superoxide-producing NADPH-oxidase complex genes were induced by TRAF3 KO.
source: Superoxide-producing NADPH-oxidase complex genes, which eliminate bacteria and fungi, were also induced (Figure 6G), as were several chemokines and growth factors (Figure 6H), but some genes that normally respond to pathogens, such as defensins, IL-8, and IL-17, were not affected.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data shown in heatmaps.

claim: Several chemokines and growth factors were induced by TRAF3 KO.
source: Superoxide-producing NADPH-oxidase complex genes, which eliminate bacteria and fungi, were also induced (Figure 6G), as were several chemokines and growth factors (Figure 6H), but some genes that normally respond to pathogens, such as defensins, IL-8, and IL-17, were not affected.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data shown in heatmaps.

claim: Some genes that normally respond to pathogens, such as defensins, IL-8, and IL-17, were not affected by TRAF3 KO.
source: Superoxide-producing NADPH-oxidase complex genes, which eliminate bacteria and fungi, were also induced (Figure 6G), as were several chemokines and growth factors (Figure 6H), but some genes that normally respond to pathogens, such as defensins, IL-8, and IL-17, were not affected.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data analysis.

claim: p100 KO partially reduces antigen presentation gene expression in TRAF3 KO cells.
source: We found that p100 KO partially reduces antigen presentation gene expression, the interferon response pathway, and foreign DNA and RNA recognition genes (Figure 6B–E), but differential gene expression of other pathways was not significantly changed.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNAseq data between TRAF3 KO and TRAF3/p100 double KO cells.

claim: p100 KO partially reduces the interferon response pathway in TRAF3 KO cells.
source: We found that p100 KO partially reduces antigen presentation gene expression, the interferon response pathway, and foreign DNA and RNA recognition genes (Figure 6B–E), but differential gene expression of other pathways was not significantly changed.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNAseq data between TRAF3 KO and TRAF3/p100 double KO cells.

claim: p100 KO partially reduces foreign DNA and RNA recognition genes in TRAF3 KO cells.
source: We found that p100 KO partially reduces antigen presentation gene expression, the interferon response pathway, and foreign DNA and RNA recognition genes (Figure 6B–E), but differential gene expression of other pathways was not significantly changed.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNAseq data between TRAF3 KO and TRAF3/p100 double KO cells.

claim: Antigen presentation, interferon pathways, and foreign DNA and RNA recognition genes are downstream targets of noncanonical NF-κB signaling in mammary epithelial cells.
source: These data argue that antigen presentation, interferon pathways, and foreign DNA and RNA recognition genes are downstream targets of noncanonical NF-κB signaling in mammary epithelial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAseq data showing partial rescue by p100 deletion.

claim: None of the immune response pathways activated by TRAF3 loss is likely to promote cell proliferation.
source: However, none of these pathways is likely to promote cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known functions of these pathways.

claim: Noncanonical NF-κB signaling suppresses signals that normally would cause cell cycle exit.
source: Rather, the data suggest that noncanonical NF-κB signaling instead suppresses signals that normally would cause cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no activation of proliferation pathways but prevention of quiescence.

claim: Deletion of TRAF3 did not induce significant nuclear accumulation of YAP at high density.
source: However, deletion of TRAF3 did not induce significant nuclear accumulation of YAP, as compared to the NT control (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence staining and quantification of YAP localization.

claim: More than 90% of conserved YAP target genes showed no significant induction in TRAF3 KO cells compared to the NT control.
source: Moreover, comparison of expression profiles for conserved YAP target genes (Cordenonsi et al., 2011) from our RNAseq data showed an absence of any significant induction for more than 90% of conserved YAP target genes in TRAF3 KO cells compared to the NT control (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data analysis of YAP target genes.

claim: TRAF3 loss promotes over-proliferation independently of YAP.
source: We conclude, therefore, that TRAF3 loss promotes over-proliferation independently of YAP, a major regulator of cell density-dependent proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the YAP localization and target gene expression data.

claim: The over-proliferation phenotype caused by TRAF3 KO is cell autonomous.
source: However, there was no significant difference in the fraction of KI-67+ cells between NT GFP cells mixed with NT mScarlet and NT GFP cells mixed with TRAF3 KO mScarlet cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). These data strongly argue that the over-proliferation phenotype is cell autonomous and is not a consequence of secreted cytokines or other factors.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-culture experiments with labeled cells.

claim: The over-proliferation phenotype is not a consequence of secreted cytokines or other factors.
source: However, there was no significant difference in the fraction of KI-67+ cells between NT GFP cells mixed with NT mScarlet and NT GFP cells mixed with TRAF3 KO mScarlet cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). These data strongly argue that the over-proliferation phenotype is cell autonomous and is not a consequence of secreted cytokines or other factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-culture experiment data.

claim: p21 levels were low in cells at low density, but were high in all dense cultures, irrespective of TRAF3 or p100 expression.
source: p21 levels were low in cells at low density, but were high in all dense cultures, irrespective of TRAF3 or p100 expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: No significant changes in p27, p18, or p19 were detected at low versus high cell density, or in the absence of TRAF3 or p100.
source: No significant changes in any of the other CKIs we tested were detected at low versus high cell density, or in the absence of TRAF3 or p100 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A'–C').
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blotting experiments.

claim: Noncanonical NF-κB signaling overrides the ability of CKIs to induce cell cycle arrest in EpH4 cells.
source: These data argue that noncanonical NF-κB signaling overrides the ability of these CKIs to induce cell cycle arrest in EpH4 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CKI western blotting data showing no changes despite over-proliferation.

claim: TRAF3 induces over-proliferation by triggering CYCLIN D1 expression.
source: It was previously shown that TRAF3 induces over-proliferation by triggering CYCLIN D1 expression (Demicco et al., 2005; Park et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2007; Cao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A small increase in CYCLIN D1 levels was observed in TRAF3 KO cells compared to control.
source: We analyzed CYCLIN D1 in dense TRAF3 KO cells compared to NT cells by immunofluorescence. Indeed, we observed a small increase in CYCLIN D1 levels in TRAF3 KO cells compared to control (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence staining and quantification.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 prevents cells from entering the G0 quiescent state.
source: We hypothesized that loss of TRAF3 prevents cells from entering the G0 quiescent state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in subsequent experiments.

claim: Starvation decreased proliferation in control cells but not in TRAF3 KO cells.
source: We observed no difference in proliferation between NT and TRAF3 KO cells in normal medium after 1 day post-confluency. However, starvation decreased proliferation in control cells but not in TRAF3 KO cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BrdU incorporation assays under starvation conditions.

claim: Loss of TRAF3 prevents cells from entering G0 under starvation conditions.
source: These data suggest that loss of TRAF3 prevents cells from entering G0.
evidence: This is an inference based on the starvation experiment data.

claim: At high density, control cells enter quiescence with almost exclusive nuclear localization of DHB-mVenus.
source: As shown in Figure 8E and F, at high density control cells enter quiescence, with almost exclusive nuclear localization of the biosensor.
evidence: This is demonstrated through DHB-mVenus localization experiments.

claim: Cells lacking TRAF3 show an increased percent of cytoplasmic DHB-mVenus localization at high density.
source: In contrast, cells lacking TRAF3 show an increased percent of cytoplasmic DHB-mVenus localization at high density, consistent with them continuing in cycle instead of entering quiescence.
evidence: This is demonstrated through DHB-mVenus localization experiments.

claim: RB phosphorylation was very low in NT control at high density but loss of TRAF3 induced a dramatic increase in phospho-RB positive cells.
source: RB phosphorylation was very low in NT control at high density but loss of TRAF3 induced a dramatic increase in phospho-RB positive cells (Figure 8E and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phospho-RB staining and quantification.

claim: The key effect of loss of TRAF3 is a failure to enter G0 under conditions that normally promote quiescence.
source: Together, these data strongly argue that the key effect of loss of TRAF3 is a failure to enter G0 under conditions that normally promote quiescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DHB-mVenus and phospho-RB data.

claim: Low Traf3 mRNA expression is associated with significantly worse survival for lung cancer patients.
source: Interestingly, however, genetic alterations in Traf3 occur in a variety of human epithelial cancers, though at a level of <6% (Zhu et al., 2018). Low Traf3 mRNA expression is also associated with significantly worse survival for lung and gastric cancer patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Nagy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis data shown in the figure and supported by a citation.

claim: Low Traf3 mRNA expression is associated with significantly worse survival for gastric cancer patients.
source: Interestingly, however, genetic alterations in Traf3 occur in a variety of human epithelial cancers, though at a level of <6% (Zhu et al., 2018). Low Traf3 mRNA expression is also associated with significantly worse survival for lung and gastric cancer patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Nagy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis data shown in the figure and supported by a citation.

claim: Genetic alterations in Traf3 occur in a variety of human epithelial cancers at a level of <6%.
source: Interestingly, however, genetic alterations in Traf3 occur in a variety of human epithelial cancers, though at a level of <6% (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.
